title: National school exam digitization rollout
source_ref: dst/National School System Exam Digitization Rollout.md
summary: A country wants to replace paper-based final secondary-school exams with a digital exam system.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.narrative: These objectives are not perfectly aligned. Stronger security can reduce usability, faster grading can create legitimacy concerns, and full digitization can improve efficiency while widening regional inequity if readiness is uneven.

entries.text: equal fairness across schools and regions

sections.title: Capabilities
sections.narrative: These capabilities interact tightly. Some require others, some create new vulnerabilities, and some only become useful when governance and operational dependencies are already in place.

entries.text: secure student login and identity verification

sections.title: Dependencies
sections.narrative: Many of these dependencies are jointly necessary and owned by different actors.

entries.text: every school has sufficient functioning devices
internet connectivity or offline sync readiness
legal approval of digital exam results
dispute-resolution process updated for digital evidence
interoperability between ministry, vendor, and regional systems works

sections.title: Constraints
sections.narrative: These are admissibility-shaping constraints, not optional preferences.

entries.text: national law requires equal treatment across all exam candidates
no student may be disadvantaged by disability, region, or school wealth
high-stakes exams must be legally challengeable and auditable
exam content must remain confidential before the sitting
the exam must proceed even under partial technical failure
budget caps prohibit replacing all school hardware at once
unions limit invigilator workflow changes without training
some regions prohibit external cloud hosting of student data
schools cannot suspend all legacy processes immediately
national results calendar cannot slip beyond a fixed deadline

sections.title: Boundaries
sections.narrative: These boundaries are where coordination friction and design mismatch appear.

sections.title: States
sections.narrative: The transition is not a single linear upgrade. Some states are target-like, some are mixed, some are degraded, and some are crisis states.

entries.text: limited pilot digital exams in selected schools
mixed-mode national operation, some digital and some paper
digital exams with offline local resilience
fully digital centralized real-time exam operation
digitally integrated target state with audited fallback capacity
degraded emergency state using paper fallback during system failure
legally contested state after exam irregularity
regionally asymmetric state where some regions are compliant and others are not
move from paper-only to digital authoring but paper sitting
expand pilot digital exams to selected schools
move from pilot to mixed-mode nationwide digital-paper coexistence
move directly from paper-only to full digital delivery
add offline caching and local continuity capability
centralize all live submissions in real time
revert from digital exam session to emergency paper fallback
split rollout by region according to readiness
delay deployment and preserve paper while dependencies are repaired
enable anomaly detection and digital audit trail
legal remediation transition after contested results

candidate_paths.title: Path A: conservative layering
candidate_paths.narrative:
Interpretation: digitize authoring first, then pilot, then scale.

Strength: lower operational shock.

Risk: mixed-mode drift, legal inconsistency, uneven fairness.

candidate_paths.title: Path B: resilience-first modernization
candidate_paths.narrative:
Interpretation: do not go fully digital until offline resilience, accessibility, and fallback are built.

Strength: strong continuity and legitimacy.

Risk: slower, more expensive, politically frustrating.

candidate_paths.title: Path C: direct leap
candidate_paths.narrative:
Interpretation: national big-bang full digital switch.

Strength: fastest structural simplification.

Risk: catastrophic if dependencies are uneven.

candidate_paths.title: Path D: regional rollout
candidate_paths.narrative:
Interpretation: different regions adopt at different speeds.

Strength: realistic under uneven infrastructure.

Risk: fairness and legitimacy conflict at national scale.

candidate_paths.title: Path E: pilot then stall
candidate_paths.narrative:
Interpretation: the system becomes permanently mixed-mode.

Strength: short-term convenience.

Risk: the transformation fails to converge.

This is often the real-world failure mode.
